text.ep_meas: Each rank sends 64 tokens × 2 = 128 rows of 256 numbers (65,536 bytes in BF16), but receives between 114 and 141: the busiest rank does 1.10 times the mean expert work. 26% of the copies stay on their own rank. The distributed output equals the one-process layer bit for bit (maximum difference 0.0).
text.s7_answer: Sends are balanced by construction (every rank sends T · k = 128 rows), receives are not: 114 to 141 rows, because receiving is set by how popular each rank's experts are. In a real deployment that rank finishes last and every other rank waits for it in the combine.
text.s0_meas: Held-out loss (20 fixed validation batches): dense 2.278; 8 experts top 2 2.256; 16 + 1 shared top 3 2.210, at the same active FFN size and 2.6 to 2.8 times the parameters. Balancing by bias 2.230 against aux loss 2.256; no balancing 2.296 with MaxVio 1.88 against 0.12.
text.s2_topk_answer: Measured on 10 held-out batches (CPU): k = 1 gives 2.530, the trained k = 2 2.244, k = 3 2.252, k = 4 2.269. Dropping to one expert hurts most: the model learned to spread each token over two experts and to rely on the second's contribution. More experts do not help either: most likely because the experts and the layers after them were trained against the k = 2 mixture and never saw a third or fourth output at that weight.
text.mis_topk: Changing k after training changes the function: the trained moe8top2 model gives 2.244 at its k = 2, 2.530 at k = 1 (half the expert compute) and 2.269 at k = 4 (measured, 10 held-out batches). Published MoE results that vary k at inference (DeepSeekMoE's Figure 5) do so on models with many small experts; check on your own held-out set before shipping it.
text.s3_none: The run with balancing switched off (balance=none, everything else equal) ends with MaxVio 1.88 averaged over its 6 layers, against 0.12 with the auxiliary loss; in its worst layer (3) one expert takes 48% of all assignments, and 14 of its 48 experts get under 1% of the traffic. Its held-out loss is 2.296 against 2.256: higher.
text.s3_auxbias: Held-out loss and MaxVio after 1,500 steps: softmax router with the auxiliary loss 2.256 and 0.12; softmax router with the bias instead 2.265 and 0.06; sigmoid router with the bias (DeepSeek-V3's recipe) 2.230 and 0.04. The softmax pair differs only in the balancing switch; the seed-1 rerun of the aux-loss model (2.254) sets the noise to read these gaps against.
text.s3_bias_answer: The largest bias in the sigmoid-plus-bias model after 1,500 steps is 0.074 in magnitude (measured). Each step moves every bias by exactly 0.001 up or down, so 1,500 steps bound it at 1.5; an expert that is persistently over- or under-loaded drifts steadily, while a balanced one oscillates around a fixed value. Against sigmoid scores in (0, 1), a bias of this size is enough to override the router for near-ties.
text.s4_meas: The moe8top2 model (trained dropless) evaluated on 10 held-out batches: dropless 2.244; capacity factor 2.0 2.244 (0.0% of assignments dropped); 1.25 2.252 (0.0%); 1.0 2.514 (3.1%); 0.5 6.051 (50.0%, and 47.1% of tokens lost both experts). The model trained with capacity factor 1.0 (and so with drops in every training step) is 2.310 on its own training rule against 2.256 for the dropless model, and evaluated dropless it reaches 2.276.
text.s4_batch: The same model and the same 2 × 32 held-out sequences at capacity factor 1.25, cut into batches of 32, 4 and 1 sequences: 0.0%, 0.2% and 1.8% of assignments dropped, held-out loss 2.179, 2.195 and 2.242 (measured). With 256 tokens per batch the average expert gets 64 assignments and a capacity of 80; random fluctuation over that small a sample overflows far more often than over 8,192 tokens.

text.s5_meas: 16 experts of width 256 plus one shared, top 3 (the same active FFN and 5% more total parameters than moe8top2): held-out 2.210 against 2.256 for 8 experts top 2 and 2.278 dense. DeepSeekMoE's shared-expert ablation, repeated on the trained model at inference: switching the shared expert off raises the loss to 3.863, and routing one more expert in its place to 3.850 (from 2.210; the model was not retrained, unlike DeepSeekMoE's 1.808 to 2.414, so this measures how much the trained model leans on it). Masking each token's best routed expert (DeepSeekMoE's redundancy test) raises the loss by 1.685 for the fine-grained model and 2.811 for moe8top2: the opposite direction to DeepSeekMoE's Figure 4 (does not reproduce), though here the masked expert is one of 3 routed choices against one of 2, so the two numbers are not a matched comparison.
text.probe: 5,165 tokens/s against 16,300 for the batched forward, median over a 40-step probe each; the loop calls nonzero() once per expert per layer, and every call waits for the GPU
text.s6_meas: Held-out loss: dense 2.278, 8 experts top 2 2.256, 16 + 1 shared top 3 2.210. Seed spread: moe8top2 seed 0 and 1: 2.256 and 2.254; dense seed 0 and 1: 2.278 and 2.264. So the 8-expert model's gain over dense (0.022) is about the size of the dense seed-to-seed spread (0.014) and should not be read as more than a lean; the fine-grained model's gain (0.068) is several times that spread. Both store 2.6 to 2.8 times the dense parameters for the same active FFN. Rough speed on this laptop: dense 40,091 tokens/s, moe8top2 15,045 with the batched forward; the tiny GPT's original per-expert loop is slower still (5,165 tokens/s against 16,300 for the batched forward, median over a 40-step probe each; the loop calls nonzero() once per expert per layer, and every call waits for the GPU).
text.s9_trends: Experts per layer went from 8 to 16 (Mixtral, Jamba, early 2024) to 128 to 896 (14 of the 15 models from July 2025 on have 128 or more); expert width fell from 3.5 times d (Mixtral) to 0.25 to 0.5 times d; routers moved to sigmoid scores with a selection bias in the DeepSeek line and the many models built on its code (Kimi, GLM, MiniMax, Nemotron), while Qwen kept softmax with a global-batch loss; most keep one shared expert and the first 1 to 3 layers dense; and the 2026 models add tricks around the experts rather than inside them: hash-routed first layers (DeepSeek-V4-Pro), latent projections (Nemotron 3 Super, Kimi K3), FP4 experts (DeepSeek-V4-Pro's expert_dtype).
text.mis_special: Measured on the tiny GPT (moe8top2, 40,960 held-out tokens): given only the token id, its most common first-choice expert is right 77% to 98% of the time depending on the layer, against 12.5% for an id-blind router: routing is largely a function of the token itself (the expert-to-token table is below).
